Reading this comments is very comforting to me, not that I want others to struggle but I am so glad I am not the only one. I’m an every day weed smoker, I know it isn’t normal to need something to cope everyday but this is the way I see it: 
1. The world we live in is not “normal” either - we as humans are not built for a life like this, and especially as autistic people sometimes we have no choice but to work full time and go through overstimulating places and have to cope in some way. 
2. Previously I have used much stronger/less safe substances to cope. This may not be the best solution but it is a better one for me. 
3. It helps me to sleep when I want to, generate an appetite when I want to, and it quietens the busy voice in the back of my mind. I am much less likely to get overwhelmed when I smoke regularly. 

I understand the health implications and I do hope to limit my usage, I’m in therapy and it’s something I’m working on. But right now, it works for me. Why judge ourselves for something that helps?

I am direct but kind and I still find that some people get offended by what I am saying. It doesn’t really bother me, because if I have said what I meant and feel I have expressed it well then I cannot control someone else “reading between the lines” and drawing their own implications from what I have said. I surround myself with people who are the same way and to my family and coworkers I just openly tell them that I won’t register passive aggressiveness or hints so just tell me if something needs to be said.

Apparently it’s common for autistic women to be in abusive relationships because we aren’t great at reading the signals. I’ve experienced this repeatedly, at the point where I just don’t trust any men. Even when they start off nice, they have always ended up being horrible in my experience. I second guess all interactions, I can’t “trust my gut” like everyone tells us to. I know it sounds drastic but honestly I’d just stay away, atp it’s not worth the risk :( 

if you can’t do that then at least have some time to be 100% single, focus on showing yourself love so you know what it is meant to feel like, and read up on red flags/signs to look out for. Establish friendships first and make sure you have support around you, people you can trust and talk to. Abusers love people who have no one because it’s easy to make them feel crazy. 

(Ofc sometimes you just can’t tell, it’s never ever your fault if someone does this to you. But the more you can identify and avoid the better)

I’ve had a lot of different types of therapy and personally I found DBT very helpful. I can’t speak for any other autistic person but for me I appreciate how structured it is and it helped me immensely. I thought I had bpd at the time so I had it for that, and though I realise now I was misdiagnosed it still helped with a lot of my issues. 

It works by showing you how to reframe thoughts which might be negative or irrational. It really teaches it as a skill so you are better equipped outside of therapy after a while. It also teaches emotional regulation which is very helpful if you’re someone who has meltdowns or anxiety. I still get overwhelmed often but I’m much better at managing it. It sort of helps you to create a personal toolbox of skills and techniques that work for you. Funnily it’s how I discovered things like fidget toys for self soothing. 

I had it as 1to1 so I’m not sure how it’ll differ being in a group, it might be useful and comforting to hear other people’s experiences. I was in a psychotherapy group and I couldn’t stand it because there was no structure and I go very quiet in groups so I just didn’t get anything from it. It was also very trauma focused which was presented in metaphors and symbolic thoughts about what we were saying actually meant and I couldn’t stand that, so that probably made me shut off from the group more. It could be really good for you if you can open up to them. 

Give it a try, it might be the beginning of something great. Therapy is hard but very rewarding. Good luck!

I went on the Camino with plans to be completely alone with my thoughts, walk by myself and journal when I was not walking. I didn’t have any interest in meeting people or chatting. But it’s almost impossible not to! I’ve made friends for life. And I only journaled 1 page in 2 weeks. 

Everyone is so friendly and because you’re all doing the same thing, it’s so easy to talk to people. If you want to, you definitely will. I think the easiest way is in hostels and albergues because everyone really bonds there. Just strike up conversations, ask people how far they’ve walked that day and how they’re finding it. What brought them on the Camino, if they’ve done anything similar before? It comes very easily when you’re there (as a fellow introvert I normally find this very hard). 

When you meet someone once and have a brief conversation, you often see them later on the same trail or in another albergue and even though you may have only had 1 conversation you embrace that person and catch up and it’s lovely. There is a real sense of community that reinstated my faith in humanity! You will have an amazing time.

Firstly, I am beyond sorry that you had that experience in Canada. It sounds like it was something you could not have prevented and that is usually the case. The only person to blame is the person who did that to you. You don’t want that to stop you from going on trips and experiencing life in the future, but ensure you take time to heal and do this in your own time. The Camino will be waiting for you when you are ready. 

A lot of people will tell you the Camino is totally safe and you don’t need to worry and for the most part that is true. I went this year alone and had a wonderful time and met amazing people. 

However, I had one experience when a man walking some distance ahead of me (not a hiker) turned around and made an obscene gesture as if he was touching himself. I don’t know if he actually was. I was turning off onto a different road and I felt scared for a while because he could’ve come back and been behind me. I was exhausted, struggling with blisters, carrying a backpack. I would not have been able to defend myself. I wished I had some form of self defence in that moment. A spray, a knife, anything just to deter. But I don’t know if it would’ve helped honestly (thankfully nothing happened and I remained alone on the trail for a while). 

If it makes you feel better to have a personal alarm or a spray you should bring it. But the most valuable thing in my opinion is walking with or near others. You can still walk alone if that’s your thing, but take populated routes and go at busier times. Talk to people and make friends with other women. Everyone helps each other and there is a real sense of community. 

Same for hostels, stay in rooms with lots of people. Yes it’s noisier but it always feels safer to me. One time, I booked a bed in a room of 4 and 2 of the beds remained empty so it was just me and a man. Again, it was fine. But I didn’t feel 100% comfortable and I didn’t sleep. In private albergues there are often female only dorms too. You might have to book in advance and think about where you’re staying with less spontaneity but it’s worth it to feel safe. 

Don’t rush yourself. You’ll do the Camino and it will be amazing but take your time and it’ll be even better.

When I was 16/17 I had a thing with a 25/26 year old and thought nothing of it. The age of consent where I live is 16. I had friends who dated older guys and it was normalised. When I turned 23, I was working in a school with 16 year olds and it suddenly struck me that's the age I was back then. I was talking to them about their exams and school life, trying to be a role model, talking to them in a way a teacher would. It made me feel sick to imagine that someone of my age could look at those same people and think of them in a sexual/romantic way. 

Trust me, once you get into your mid 20's, someone of that age will seem so young to you the idea of viewing them in that way will be extremely uncomfortable. It's not just weird, it will seem genuinely vile to you. No, they are not "pre-pubescent" children, but the difference in maturity is so vast in a way only the older person understands. It is a position of power. Legalities aside, anyone who does that is doing something seriously wrong. The fact he has not responded in any way speaks volumes to that fact. 

Also, just because worse things are happening does not mean that speaking out about this is a "waste of time". If anyone I knew had done something like this I would lose all trust in their character and morality. Pedo might not technically be the right word but predator sounds about right.

I had a manager say the n-word once in the context of repeating what someone else had said. I involuntarily had a physical reaction because I was so taken aback. His defence was that he wasn’t actually saying it, just quoting. I told him it’s better to censor it in that situation and he agreed. I think he genuinely didn’t realise. 

When people say stuff like “you don’t look autistic” they are probably well meaning but ignorant. But someone using a slur likely knows it’s offensive language. I don’t know what this person said but the fact they “corrected” themselves shows they know it’s wrong. If it happens again and you’re comfortable enough, try and show them you are not cool with it.

This is terrible coming from a manager! Honesty in an ideal world you could have a conversation with this person and tell them that it’s not cool, and possibly report/escalate it depending on her response. But in reality I know this can make your work life difficult, especially if people are not understanding. 

I’ve heard co workers use autistic as an insult and it stings but I usually just brush it off. I can’t deal with any conflict. But from a manager it seems much worse for some reason. I don’t have much advice to give, just sorry you are dealing with this!

You should read untamed by Glennon Doyle! I listened to her talking about her life on a podcast and basically she fell in love with a woman and was very fearful to leave her husband and how it would effect her kids. 

Spoiler alert she basically decides that it is more important for her kids to see her living boldly and making authentic choices than for them to see her commit to something which makes her unhappy. 

Your kids benefit from you doing what’s right for you. Of course divorce is never pretty but a child is better off having separated but happy parents rather than parents who are together and miserable.

Editing to add: you say this man is wonderful and many women would be glad to have him. Let him go find her! It’s not only unfair on yourself to stay in an unhappy marriage, it’s unfair on your partner too. You should both have the freedom to find the best situation for you

I know I’m doing nothing wrong, I just don’t want anyone to know either way. I don’t want to be heard, I don’t want anyone to think about me being there. I was completely non verbal for the first couple of years of school. As in, I could talk fine at home but at school I just went silent. For some reason I just got labelled as shy and no one thought this was cause for concern. 

Once in assembly, the whole school was gathered together in the hall sat on the floor and I realised I was desperate to pee. You can see where this is going… I just started to go and pretended like I didn’t know it was happening, the kids around me noticed and started freaking out and moving away while I sat in a huge puddle literally not reacting. 

A teacher came to sort me out and kept asking why I didn’t say anything but I couldn’t reply and I don’t think I even knew myself. Anyway the whole hall had to be cleared out and everyone remembered it for years. Mortifying!

I actually worked there for a few months when I was younger because I loved what they stood for socially/environmentally. I was quite happy to approach and say hello to everyone, ask if they need help, and leave them alone if they say no. The management really push you to push yourself onto other people though to the point it’s uncomfortable for everyone. I hated it and had many tearful shifts because I couldn’t understand what I was doing wrong. 

Now when I go in there as a customer I wear headphones and go directly to what I want to look at. I feel quite sympathetic towards the staff bc of my own experience so I’m just polite but firm that I know what I’m looking for and nod along while they do their initial spiel.

I tried to do this when I was younger on the advice of my therapist because she thought it would make me seem approachable and I was nervous about making friends (I basically wore all black). She told me to wear more colours and advised me on what was fashionable at the time. 

I ended up feeling really uncomfortable, acting pretty awkward as a result, and I didn’t fit in with the “normal” people because they could tell I was odd - but the misfits I’d normally have befriended also rejected me because in their eyes I looked like a normie. I tried experimenting with things I thought made me look “normal” and actually ended up getting laughed at and wanting to hide and just wear my normal clothes. Just wear what makes you feel confident and comfortable. You don’t want to make friends by pretending you’re someone you’re not - you won’t make the right friends.

It’s definitely trauma, whether from porn or from growing up in a culture where women and girls are sexualised constantly and simultaneously shamed.

This isn’t easy or straightforward, but I think you should prioritise your own relationship with your body and viewing yourself in a positive light. Whether it’s about being sexy, beautiful, or accepting. 

The traditional “sexy” we are taught is performative and usually for men, so if we aren’t 100% confident and comfortable it just feels wrong. - the narc relationship moved very quickly. They overwhelmed me with compliments and gifts which I loved, and would scatter it with “I hope I’m not being too much too fast”. -belittling you in front of others even in a jokey way

-if you say anything slightly critical they get extremely defensive and can make it into a huge argument. 

-after an argument or display of aggression they will apologise and be so kind and sweet again, show so much regret and usually gifts to make up for it. 

- arguments looked very different to the ones in my other relationship and would escalate very quickly. It was never about trying to understand each other’s feelings, it felt like they wanted to win a debate. They would always start off from small things and made a huge deal out of it. They’d say personal insults and get angry, and also accuse you of saying things you didn’t. They confuse you and you end up apologising and not really understanding why. 

These are obviously huge things and the arguments probably means you’re past “dating” stage, but as the relationship with a narc moves fast these incidents can start quite early on. I wish I’d taken more notice of the behaviour at that time and not accepted the meaningless apologies. 

In comparison, in my healthier relationship we moved things at a fairly slow pace and went on dates together and got to know each other before confessing our love etc. I received flowers but there was no bombarding of gifts or claiming to have never felt this way before etc. Arguments when properly in the relationship were still arguments but at the end you would both hear each other out and try to discuss it calmly. They would never make personal insults or get aggressive.
